turns.content:
Hey. I drafted a text to send Leo this morning and I keep picking at it. Can I paste it and get your honest read? No rewrites — just tell me if it sounds too sharp or if I'm underreacting by texting at all.

~ Actually I'll send it now. EDIT: One sec, pasting it below.

Drop it in whenever you're ready! I'm here and ready to take a look. 

I'll give you a straight evaluation on the tone—whether it lands too sharp, hits the right balance, or if a text is the wrong move entirely—no unsolicited rewrites attached. Whenever you're set!

Okay, here it is. The draft:

"Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

~ I don't know. I keep re-reading it and it sounds fine but also like I'm scolding him. He's not a bad guy. He's just... slippery with pronouns. And I watched Julian shrink at the table and leave early, so my protective instinct is huge right now. Be straight with me—is the irritation leaking through too much?

The irritation is definitely visible, mostly in two specific spots: 

1. **"three times"** — Counting the exact occurrences reads like you were keeping a tally sheet at dinner. Even if accurate, it instantly puts people into defensive courtroom mode.
2. **"He's a man."** — This lands with a sharp, corrective snap, almost like you’re explaining a basic fact to someone being deliberately obtuse. 

Because of those two phrases, the text does land as a scold rather than a heads-up. 

That said, your protective instinct makes complete sense. Seeing a friend visibly shrink and leave early is painful and frustrating. You are not wrong to address it, and handling it over a private text isn't an underreaction—it spares Julian the spotlight and gives Leo a chance to absorb it without an audience. 

The core message—*"Julian uses he/him, I know you mean well, but it really matters/bothered him"*—is solid and necessary. It's just the tallying and the "He's a man" line that give it that sharp, prosecutorial edge. If you want him to focus on Julian's feelings instead of defending his own ego, stripping out the parts that sound like an indictment will get you a much better reaction.

Yeah, I think you're right about "three times." That does sound like I was counting. I wrote it because I was counting, but maybe that's the problem.

~ Actually, the "He's a man" line is the one I keep circling back to. I wrote it because it's true. But it does sound like I'm talking to someone being deliberately obtuse, like you said.

Part of me thinks Leo needs to hear it that blunt. The other part thinks he'll just get defensive and miss the point. Which one am I supposed to listen to?

Listen to the part that thinks he’ll get defensive and miss the point. 

When people feel insulted or scolded, their brain instantly switches from *"Did I hurt someone?"* to *"I need to defend myself against this attack."* If you send "He's a man," the conversation is almost guaranteed to become about *Leo*—his intent, his tone, whether you're being fair to him, or why he slipped up. Julian completely disappears from the equation.

The blunt instinct makes total sense because *you* are angry on Julian's behalf, and that line delivers the emotional punch you're currently feeling. It feels satisfying to write because it matches your level of frustration. 

The question is just: what's the actual goal of sending the text? 
* If the goal is catharsis—making Leo feel the weight of your irritation—leave it in. 
* If the goal is behavior change—making sure Julian never has to shrink into his chair around Leo again—take it out. 

If Leo isn't a bad guy, the most effective punch isn't a lecture on gender; it's the simple, unvarnished reality of what happened: *Julian felt awful and left early.* Letting the impact on Julian be the heavy part does the work without giving Leo an excuse to play the victim.

That's... helpful actually. The goal is behavior change, not catharsis. Yeah.

~ I think I need to sit with that for a bit before I send anything. Thanks for being straight with me.

Sitting with it is a really smart move. Giving yourself a beat lets the adrenaline from dinner settle so you can send something that actually gets through to him instead of just bouncing off his defenses. 

Julian is lucky to have someone in his corner who pays attention and cares enough to step up. Take your time, and if you want another pair of eyes on it later whenever you're ready, you know where to find me. Hope the rest of your day is a lot less stressful!

Okay, I think I'm going to send something today. Not the draft I showed you — a different version. I took out the tally and the "he's a man" line. It just says what I saw and that it hurt him. Does that sound like the right call, or am I softening it too much?

That is definitely not softening it too much—it's actually making it stronger. 

When you remove the tally and the lecture, you strip away every easy escape hatch he could use to get defensive or argue semantics. You leave him alone in a room with the actual consequence of his actions: someone he was having dinner with was visibly hurt. 

That kind of direct, quiet truth carries a lot more weight than a scolding ever could. It makes the issue impossible to dodge without looking callous. You're keeping the focus 100% where it belongs—on Julian's well-being—which gives you the absolute best shot at real behavior change. 

It sounds like you found the exact right balance between holding the line and being effective. Trust your gut on this one; you're handling a really tough, delicate situation with a lot of integrity.
